title: Devananda Pandita
html:
Reciter of the “Bhagavatam”

In the “Chaitanya-charitamrita,” in the list of the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks of him in a single line:

“Devananda, the reciter of the Bhagavata, is an offshoot of Vakreshvara's branch. By Vakreshvara's mercy he received from the Lord the devotional meaning of the Bhagavata.” (CC, Adi 10.77)

Devananda Pandita was a bhagavati, one who reads and expounds the “Bhagavatam.” This one line holds his whole story: a learned expounder of the holy book did not know its essence until he served a devotee of the Lord, and then the Lord Himself revealed to him that the essence of the “Bhagavatam” is bhakti.1

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“Sri Devananda Pandita, the knower of the meaning of the Puranas, was formerly the sage Bhaguri, the pandit of Nanda's assembly.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 106)

So too Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in his “Anubhashya” to CC, Adi 10.77: in Vraja he is Bhaguri Muni, the pandit of Nanda Maharaja's court.2

Little is known of his worldly life. He was a brahmana; the sources name neither his parents nor his family, nor the year of his appearance or departure.

Navadvipa and Kuliya

Vrindavana Dasa Thakura, beginning his account of Devananda in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” tells us where he lived:

“Thus the Lord Vishvambhara came to the embankment by the house of Visharada Maheshvara, father of Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. There lived a brahmana named Devananda Pandita — supremely peaceful, and desiring liberation.” (CB, Madhya 21.6–7)

So he lived near the house of Maheshvara Visharada, father of Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, by the embankment (jangal) along which the Lord would pass. Narahari Chakravarti in the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” leading a pilgrim through the holy places of Navadvipa, points out this place too: “Here is the embankment of Visharada: here the Lord met Devananda, who had offended Srivasa; at the Lord's chastisement in words he was grieved” (BR 12.2976–2977).

The school (tol) where Devananda taught the “Bhagavatam,” according to the biographies, stood in the village of Kuliya; so also writes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” to CB, Madhya 9.98: “Devananda's school was in Kuliya.” One biography says that he also lived in Kuliya, near where the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math of Srila Sridhara Maharaja now stands.3 And in the “Anubhashya” to CC, Madhya 16.207 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta names Vidyanagara on Jahnu-dvipa, near Koladvipa — where Vidya-Vachaspati's house stood — as the place where he lived.

Kuliya, according to the “Gaudiya-bhashya,” was a suburb of Navadvipa on the Ganga's western shore; the town that bears the name Navadvipa today is the old Kuliya, “the place where offences are destroyed” (aparadha-bhanjaner pat). One of the biographies explains that the heart of Navadvipa then, Mayapur, lay on the eastern bank, and the old names of quarters of the present town keep the memory of this: Koler-ganj, Koler-daha, Gadkhali-kol.

Navadvipa-dhama consists of nine islands, each corresponding to one of the nine kinds of bhakti. Kuliya is Koladvipa, the island of pada-sevana, service to the Lord's feet; in common speech “Kola” became “Kuliya.” The word “kola” means a boar: here, in Satya-yuga, the Lord as Varaha showed Himself to the brahmana Vasudeva.4

A Scholar without Bhakti

Vrindavana Dasa describes Devananda with respect:

“He was intelligent, discerning, austere and detached from birth. He studied the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam,’ yet there was no devotion to the Lord in him.” (CB, Madhya 21.8)

“At that time Devananda Pandita was honoured by all as a holy and wise scholar. He always taught the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam.’ From early childhood he had taken the vow to live as a sannyasi.” (CB, Madhya 21.57–58)

He was endowed with many good qualities, peaceful by nature, and highly respected; he read the “Bhagavatam,” kept a sannyasi's vows and had been celibate from childhood. Many studied under him, and he was famed for his knowledge of the sayings of the “Bhagavatam.”

But his renunciation was not warmed by devotion. One of the biographies says that because there was no bhakti in him, his celibacy turned into an unwillingness to serve the devotees; therefore, though he kept his vows and walked the path of renunciation, he did not obtain the fruit of these virtues. Another adds that for all his learning he did not understand that the highest aim of the “Bhagavatam” is bhakti, and, aspiring to liberation, he extolled austerity and renunciation in his expositions rather than service to the Lord.5

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” judges him with care: Devananda was a smarta, yet a great scholar and ascetic; he read nothing but the “Bhagavatam,” had faith in God and mastery over his senses — he lacked only faith in Mahaprabhu. So speaks of him Vrindavana Dasa himself:

“From his very birth he was pious, detached and learned. He taught no scripture other than the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam.’ He was peaceful, restrained, master of his senses, free from greed and endowed with many other pious qualities. But he had no faith in Lord Gaurachandra.” (CB, Antya 3.482–484)

Not a villain but an ascetic and scholar who lacked one thing — bhakti: so the Vaishnava authors see him. That is what makes his story instructive.

The Offence to Srivasa

Once Srivasa Pandita came to Devananda to hear the “Bhagavatam.” Vrindavana Dasa relates:

“Srivasa's heart melted on hearing the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam,’ for every syllable of it is full of ecstatic love for Krishna. Srivasa was a maha-bhagavata brahmana, and as he listened he began to weep and sigh deeply. The wicked students said: ‘What a disturbance! Brothers, we cannot study properly, and our time is being wasted.’” (CB, Madhya 21.60–62)

The biographies add details. Srivasa, a rasika-bhakta, fell to the ground at the very first verse; tears streamed from his eyes, his voice choked, he rolled on the floor. The students shouted: “Madman! He doesn't listen properly — out with him!” — and dragged him out by force. They came to Devananda only for knowledge of grammar and worldly recognition, and so they did not understand Srivasa's bhajana. His weeping would not stop, and they never understood that this man, so dear to Chaitanya, purifies the world, that the sattvika-bhavas of his spiritual body bring all purity to the world; taking him for an ordinary emotional man, they put him out of the classroom so that the lesson could go on.

“Srivasa could not stop his tears. And though he was a close friend of Sri Chaitanya, able to deliver the whole universe, the wicked students together pushed him out into the street. Devananda Pandita did not stop them. When the guru has no desire to serve God, his disciples become the same. Returning to outer consciousness, Srivasa went home sad.” (CB, Madhya 21.63–66)

Devananda saw this and did not stop his students — and so became guilty of vaishnava-aparadha, an offence against a devotee. One of the biographies remarks that a disciple's sin committed through his teacher's ignorance falls on the teacher too. Another says it more plainly: had Devananda been even slightly inclined to serve God, he would not have let his ignorant students do such a thing; since he did not, both he and they proved to be mere disputing reciters, lost in the sickness of sense objects. Without bhakti, vows and celibacy are fruitless: a teacher not inclined to serve the Lord will not keep his students from offence and becomes guilty himself.

Srivasa went home saddened and said nothing to anyone. According to one of the biographies, all this happened before the appearance of Sri Gauranga.6

But the Lord, who dwells in every heart, knew everything. When in Srivasa's house He revealed His glory in the mahaprakasha, He reminded Srivasa of this incident:

“Mahaprabhu said: ‘Srivasa, do you remember how you once heard the “Bhagavatam” from the mouth of Devananda Pandita? Every line of the “Bhagavatam” is full of prema-rasa, and your heart melted at those narrations. You began to weep loudly and fell to the ground, overwhelmed by ecstatic feelings. ‹…› Unconscious, you showed the signs of divine love, and the students put you out into the street. Devananda did not stop them. The guru proved as ignorant as his students.’” (CB, Madhya 9.90–95)

According to one of the biographies, the Lord then spoke of the book-bhagavata and the devotee-bhagavata, and for a long time remained indifferent to Devananda, not granting him prema.

The Rebuke

Vrindavana Dasa tells of two occasions when the Lord spoke about Devananda.7 The first time He only heard his lesson. One day the Lord was walking through Navadvipa with His devotees and passed by Visharada's house:

“By Providence the Lord and His devotees heard on their way how he was expounding the scriptures. Present in the hearts of all beings, the Lord knows everything. He did not hear the glorification of loving service to God in that exposition.” (CB, Madhya 21.11–12)

And the Lord, in anger, spoke of the “Bhagavatam”: this reciter would not grasp its meaning in any birth —

“‘The “Srimad-Bhagavatam” is Krishna Himself in the form of a book. In the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” loving service to God is described as the highest goal of life. The four Vedas proclaim the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” to be the embodiment of ecstatic love for Krishna. The four Vedas are like curd, and the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” is the butter. Shukadeva churned it, and Maharaja Parikshit tasted this nectar. My dear Shukadeva knows the conclusion of the “Srimad-Bhagavatam,” in which the science of My greatness and glory is revealed. Whoever makes a difference between Me, My servant and the book “Bhagavatam” surely brings ruin upon himself.’” (CB, Madhya 21.14–18)8

The Lord said that a reciter who, expounding the “Bhagavatam,” says nothing of loving service to God knows nothing — and set out to tear up his book; but the Vaishnavas stopped Him (CB, Madhya 21.20–22).9 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” to these verses why the Lord is angry. Those devoid of bhakti take indifference to service for the highest goal and thereby irritate the Lord, though by nature He is merciful. Gaurasundara shows that such a view is not merely needless but faulty, and that both enjoying the fruits of one's actions and renouncing them are out of place. The Lord's anger gladdens the devotees: it is not like the anger of a conditioned soul; it is His care for the purity of bhakti.

Then the Lord said:

“All the scriptures glorify the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ as the highest spiritual work, yet such understanding does not come through erudition, austerity or fame. If someone thinks, ‘I have understood the “Srimad-Bhagavatam,”’ he in fact does not know the conclusions of this holy book. But one who accepts the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ as a manifestation of the inconceivable Lord understands that its meaning is pure loving service to God.” (CB, Madhya 21.23–25)

One of the biographies renders these words thus: the “Bhagavatam” is not understood by learning and austerity, but only by bhakti; whoever wishes to understand it must serve both the book-bhagavata and the devotee-bhagavata. Having said this, the Lord went home with His devotees. Devananda heard it all from afar but paid it no heed.

The second time the Lord met him face to face:

“Walking about, Gaurachandra met Devananda Pandita and addressed him in anger. The Lord remembered how Devananda Pandita had earlier offended Srivasa Pandita.” (CB, Madhya 21.53–54)

It was by that same embankment of Visharada (BR 12.2976–2977). The Lord sternly rebuked Devananda for having no faith in the Vaishnavas: by indulging his students, hostile to Srivasa, he had lost the right to read the “Bhagavatam.” According to the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” at that very time Saranga Thakura met the Lord in a street of Navadvipa.10

“‘Devananda, I want to tell you something. Now you teach everyone the “Srimad-Bhagavatam.” Once Srivasa, whom the Ganga herself longs to see, came to you to hear the “Srimad-Bhagavatam.” What was his fault, that you and your students put him out of your house? Is it right to drive out one who weeps with love for Krishna while hearing the “Srimad-Bhagavatam”?’” (CB, Madhya 21.67–71)

In the retelling of one of the biographies the Lord said: hearing the “Bhagavatam” sung melts the heart; only those attached to worldly enjoyment keep it hard; when Srivasa gave himself wholly to devotional feeling, neither you nor your students understood him, and you drove him away from the hearing; yet even the Ganga, who stands on Hara's head, came down to earth as a river to see such a devotee; this offence has justly made you averse to God.

“Though you expound the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam,’ I am convinced that you will not understand its meaning in any of your future lives.” (CB, Madhya 21.72)

An expounder of the “Bhagavatam,” he had not in any birth gained the sukriti — the piety — that would let him grasp its meaning.

Mercy in the Form of Punishment

Vrindavana Dasa closes the account thus:

“Hearing these words of the Lord, the exalted brahmana Devananda Pandita felt deep shame and said nothing in reply. Having spoken such angry words, Vishvambhara went away, and Devananda returned home dejected. That the Lord Himself rebuked him shows Devananda's great good fortune. Lord Chaitanya punishes only the most fortunate. Even if a person perishes as a result of such punishment, he attains Vaikuntha.” (CB, Madhya 21.75–78)

Devananda was overcome with shame. But having received this punishment in words from the Lord, he gained the awakening of sukriti, and in time the punishment proved the source of his good fortune: great good fortune is the Lord's mercy in the form of punishment. The biographies explain Vrindavana Dasa's words: whom Vishnu punishes gains liberation; whoever is punished by Chaitanya obtains great good, and even one who would perish by His punishment goes to Vaikuntha. This speaks of what the Lord's punishment is — it always brings good; Devananda the Lord punished only with words, and it was the beginning of his deliverance.

“Whoever accepts with faith the punishment of Lord Chaitanya will surely obtain love for Krishna in the future.” (CB, Madhya 21.79)

And Vrindavana Dasa draws one more truth from this story — why the offence to Srivasa so closed the meaning of the “Bhagavatam” to Devananda:

“Krishna manifests in this world in four forms: the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam,’ Tulasi, the Ganga and the devotees of God. The worship of the Lord's Deity begins after the rite of installation; but the Vedas say that these four manifestations of the Supreme Lord are fully equal to Him from their very appearance.” (CB, Madhya 21.81–82)

One of the biographies, following the “Gaudiya-bhashya,” explains: by external reckoning, worship of the Deity begins after the rite of prana-pratishtha, while the book “Bhagavatam,” the Vaishnava, Tulasi and the Ganga are worshipped without it. Though the world sees them as objects for its own use, they are themselves enjoyers, non-different from the Lord; so say the Vedas. Therefore one who offends a devotee offends the “Bhagavatam” too — and the meaning of the book closes to him.

Meeting Vakreshvara

While the Lord lived in Navadvipa, Devananda never came to have faith in Him:

“When Gaurachandra was performing His pastimes as a householder, Devananda Pandita had no faith in Him. Therefore he could not understand the Lord. Though he was worthy of seeing the Lord, Krishna alone knows why he was unable to do so.” (CB, Antya 3.465–467)

One of the biographies relates that when the Lord had taken sannyasa and gone to Puri, Devananda remembered His teachings and began to lament: so great a personality, full of love for Krishna, had come to his very door, and he had not met Him and had not understood His glory.

And then great good fortune came to him:

“When the Lord left home and took sannyasa, Devananda Pandita had the good fortune to meet Vakreshvara Pandita.” (CB, Antya 3.468)

The Lord's dear associate Vakreshvara Pandita, by Providence, stayed in his house (CB, Antya 3.474).11 Devananda saw how devotion to Vishnu shone in him, and began to serve him with sincere love:

“While Vakreshvara Pandita danced, Devananda Pandita guarded him with a stick in his hand. Devananda himself kept the curious crowd away from him. If Vakreshvara fell unconscious, he would place his head on his lap. Lovingly he wiped the dust from Vakreshvara Pandita's body and smeared it over himself. Constant association with Vakreshvara Pandita revealed his glory to Devananda Pandita, and thus faith in Lord Chaitanya arose in Devananda.” (CB, Antya 3.477–480)

By serving Vakreshvara, Devananda became a vessel of Mahaprabhu's mercy. From Vakreshvara's lips he heard of the Lord's glory, his heart was changed, and under the influence of that company he came to love pure bhakti. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta remarks in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” that what Devananda lacked — faith in Mahaprabhu — was supplied by Vakreshvara's mercy. And Vrindavana Dasa draws from this a general rule:

“‘Service to the Vaishnavas is higher than service to Krishna’ — all the scriptures headed by the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ confirm this truth. ‘There may be doubt whether the servant of the Supreme reaches perfection, but there is no doubt that the servant of a Vaishnava reaches it.’ Therefore service to the Vaishnavas is the highest spiritual practice. By serving the Vaishnavas anyone can attain Krishna.” (CB, Antya 3.485–487)

More about how Devananda served Vakreshvara is told in the article on Vakreshvara Pandita.

Forgiveness at Kuliya

Some years after His sannyasa the Lord came from Puri to Bengal and stayed at Kuliya, across the Ganga from Nadia. Thousands flocked there, and all who had once offended Him in Navadvipa came to ask forgiveness. One of the biographies says that this was five years after His sannyasa and that the Lord then forgave everyone at the place now called aparadha-bhanjana, “the destruction of offences” — where the temple of Srila Sridhara Maharaja stands today — and taught them the science of bhakti.12

Krishnadasa Kaviraja describes this journey: because of the crowds at Vidya-Vachaspati's house the Lord went away to Kuliya and stayed in the house of Madhava Dasa; countless people saw Him there, and staying seven days He delivered all the offenders in a special way (CC, Madhya 16.207–209). Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in his “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” to these verses says plainly that in those seven days the Lord destroyed the offences of Devananda and others.

Shortly before Devananda came, the Lord gave a remedy to another brahmana who repented of having reviled the Vaishnavas:

“‘O brahmana, listen. One who has taken poison must drink nectar with the same mouth. Then the poison will be neutralized, and the nectar will make his body immortal.’” (CB, Antya 3.449–450)

With the same mouth that once offended the Vaishnavas one must now glorify them (CB, Antya 3.453).13 And right after this Devananda came:

“Lord Gaurachandra was seated when Devananda Pandita appeared before Him. Humbly offering obeisances, Devananda Pandita remained standing at a distance, hesitant. The Lord, seeing him, was pleased, and taking him aside to a quiet place, sat down with him. The Lord forgave all Devananda's former offences and bestowed His mercy on him. The Lord said: ‘You have served Vakreshvara Pandita, and that has brought you close to Me. Vakreshvara Pandita is full of the spiritual energies of the Supreme Lord. Whoever serves him attains Krishna. Krishna has made His abode in Vakreshvara's heart. When he dances, Krishna dances too. Wherever Vakreshvara stays becomes like all the holy places; Vaikuntha is manifest there.’” (CB, Antya 3.489–496)

Devananda prayed with tears:

“O all-merciful Lord! You appeared in Navadvipa to deliver the whole universe. I am sinful and unfortunate, and so I could not recognize You. Because of this I was deprived of the transcendental happiness of Your company. You are always compassionate to all living beings. Therefore I pray to You: grant me attachment to You.” (CB, Antya 3.498–500)

And he asked: “I am not all-knowing, yet I teach the book of the All-knowing, the ‘Bhagavatam,’ knowing nothing myself. Tell me what I should explain and what I should teach” (CB, Antya 3.501–503). One of the biographies renders his prayer thus: I am a sinner, I did not worship Your feet and deceived myself; but by Your causeless mercy I see Your feet; teach me what the goal of life is and explain the meaning of the “Bhagavatam.”

The Essence of the “Bhagavatam”

The Lord replied:

“‘O brahmana, listen. In teaching the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” you must explain nothing but loving service to God. In the beginning, middle and end of the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” loving service to Vishnu is described as eternally perfect, inexhaustible and flawless.’” (CB, Antya 3.505–506)

The Lord told him that the “Bhagavatam,” like the Lord's avataras, appears and disappears by its own will; that it became manifest on Vyasa's tongue by Krishna's mercy, when he was absorbed in bhakti; and that the “Bhagavatam” is not grasped by pride of learning:

“One who thinks, ‘I understand the “Srimad-Bhagavatam,”’ knows nothing of the glory of the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam.’ But even an unlettered person who takes shelter of the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ can easily understand its true meaning. The ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ is made of ecstatic divine love. It is the body of Sri Krishna. The confidential pastimes of Krishna are described there.” (CB, Antya 3.514–516)

And once more the Lord repeated the main point:

“‘You must explain loving service everywhere in the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ — in its beginning, middle and end. Then you will never commit any offence, and you will surely find joy in your heart. ‹…› Now go and teach the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam,’ explaining to everyone the bliss of loving service to Krishna.’” (CB, Antya 3.520–523)

Thus by Vakreshvara's mercy Devananda received from the Lord the devotional meaning of the “Bhagavata,” as Krishnadasa Kaviraja says (CC, Adi 10.77).

Murari Gupta tells of this meeting briefly. Devananda, who had received the mercy of Vakreshvara, came to the Lord's feet, confessed his former ill will and asked what his true good might be; and the Lord said to him: “Know that the Srimad Bhagavatam is Sri Krishna Himself, directly — the embodiment of being, consciousness and bliss, free from envy and every taint. Whoever reads it, tasting the rasa of devotion, will attain bliss.” “Hearing this, the brahmana bowed his head and, covered with the dust of His feet, immersed in the rasa of Gaurachandra, danced most wondrously” (Murari, 3.17.17–20).

The meaning of the “Bhagavatam” is open not to the proud scholar but to one who has surrendered. “Bhagavata” is both the book and the devotee, and they are one:

“There are two kinds of Bhagavata: the book Bhagavata and the person who has received Krishna's special mercy.” (CB, Antya 3.532)

One who expounds the “Bhagavatam” knowing this attains the highest good. The Lord also spoke to Devananda of the glory of Vakreshvara — the devotee-bhagavata through serving whom he came to understand the book-bhagavata.

According to one of the biographies, the Lord told Devananda to go and beg forgiveness at Srivasa's feet, for the book-bhagavata and the devotee-bhagavata are one; Devananda went at once, Srivasa embraced and forgave him, and the name of Hari resounded on all sides; from that day Devananda was accepted among Mahaprabhu's followers as a great devotee.14

Kuliya, Koladvipa, is the place where offences are destroyed, and that is why Devananda's offence too was destroyed here. Here also the Lord forgave Gopala Chapala, who had offended Srivasa (CC, Adi 17.55–59). Krishnadasa Kaviraja names both in one verse:

“In Kuliya He showed His grace to Devananda and forgave the brahmana Gopala his offence against Srivasa.” (CC, Madhya 1.153)

One of the biographies says that Devananda received this mercy because he lived in Kuliya.

The Branch of Vakreshvara and the Place of Forgiveness

Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls Devananda an offshoot of Vakreshvara Pandita's branch. According to the “Vakreshvara-charita,” one of the five branches stemming from Vakreshvara comes from Devananda.15

The place where the Lord forgave Devananda and Gopala Chapala was revealed by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura: in the month of Kartika 1922 he came to Kuliya and identified it. On this place of aparadha-bhanjana now stands the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

In Narahari Chakravarti's “Namamrita-samudra” — where he asks the Lord's associates to reveal Gaura's pastimes to him — Devananda is called by his service, “reciter of the Bhagavata”:

“Devananda, reciter of the Bhagavata! Show me that pastime — the night play in the waters of the Ganga with the devotees.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 148)

Departure

Devananda Pandita left this world on the ekadashi of the month of Pausha, in the dark half of the moon. Our calendar, the calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math, marks the day of his departure on the krishna-ekadashi of the month of Narayana, which corresponds to Pausha (Saphala Ekadashi; in 2027 it falls on January 3).16 The year and place of his departure, the place of his samadhi and the day of his appearance are not named in the sources.

Significance

Devananda's story is a lesson about vaishnava-aparadha. A scholar and ascetic, celibate from childhood, he expounded the “Bhagavatam” for years — and did not know its essence, because he did not serve the devotees and allowed an offence against a devotee. An offence to a Vaishnava closes the meaning of the “Bhagavatam” even to a scholar: “Bhagavata” is both the book and the devotee, and they are non-different from the Lord.

The Lord's anger here is not worldly anger but mercy in the form of punishment. Whom the Lord punishes, He wishes good for; the punishment in words awakened sukriti in Devananda and became the beginning of his good fortune. Taking indifference to service for the highest goal irritates the Lord, though by nature He is merciful, and Gaurasundara shows that such a view is faulty; and the devotees are gladdened by such anger of the Lord.

The “Bhagavatam” is understood not by learning but by one who has surrendered, and to understand the book-bhagavata one must serve the devotee-bhagavata. As reviling the devotees deprives one of mercy, so glorifying and serving them is the best path to mercy. An offence to a Vaishnava is removed by the forgiveness of the one offended and by service to a Vaishnava: the blessing of a devotee quickly gives bhakti. Devananda, having served Vakreshvara, gained faith in Mahaprabhu, received forgiveness, and heard from the Lord Himself that the whole essence of the “Bhagavatam” is bhakti. Not without reason does one of the biographies say that through Devananda Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu revealed the glory of the “Bhagavatam” to the world.

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesake — Devananda, one of the four brothers who were servants of Sri Nityananda: “Narayana, Krishnadasa, Manohara and Devananda — these four brothers were servants of Nitai” (CC, Adi 11.46; so too CB, Antya 5.749, 752). In the “Vaishnava-vandanas” Devananda the reciter of the “Bhagavata” and Devananda the servant of Nityananda are honoured separately.
  2. In one of the biographies the sage's name is given as “Bhandari” — an error: in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and the “Anubhashya” it is Bhaguri.
  3. These are two different statements, and they should not be merged. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Madhya 21.6–7) says that Devananda lived by the embankment of Visharada's house in Navadvipa; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” shows “Visharada's embankment” among the places of Navadvipa proper, next to the houses of Srivasa and Murari and the quarter of the drunkards, and does not place it in Kuliya. That his school was in Kuliya is inferred from the primary sources by the biographies and by the “Gaudiya-bhashya.” One of the biographies places the embankment of Visharada itself in Kuliya — this is the author's inference.
  4. This brahmana Vasudeva of Koladvipa is not Vasudeva, the leper brahmana of Kurma-kshetra whom the Lord healed during His journey through the South (CC, Madhya 7).
  5. One of the biographies calls him a great knower of the “Bhagavatam” “from the monist point of view.” The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” says only that he “desired liberation” (Madhya 21.7); we ascribe nothing more to him.
  6. According to Kavi Karnapura's “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” (act 1) and the “Prema-vilasa,” this too took place before the Lord's appearance, but it is told differently: on the day of death foretold for him, Srivasa was hearing the “Bhagavatam” about Prahlada from Devananda, fell unconscious from the veranda and was carried home; the students are not mentioned at all. According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Madhya 9, 21) the students drove out the weeping Srivasa. These are two different versions, and we do not merge them.
  7. One of the biographies merges both occasions into one scene; another gives only the first; we follow the order of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata.”

  11. So both the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Antya 3.474) and the biographies: Vakreshvara stayed in Devananda's house (ashrama). According to one of the biographies, Vakreshvara sang and danced in the house of a certain devotee in Kuliya, and Devananda came there.
  12. The sources differ on where exactly Devananda was forgiven. According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Antya 3) and the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” (Madhya 1.153) — in Kuliya. According to Murari Gupta (3.17.14–20) — in the days when the Lord was staying with Vidya-Vachaspati; so too one of the biographies: at Vachaspati's in Vidyanagara, then in Kuliya, on the way to Gauda, before meeting Rupa and Sanatana at Ramakeli. Other biographies say that the Lord stayed seven days in Kuliya in the house of Madhava Dasa (Chhakari Chattopadhyaya), father of Vamshivadana, and instructed Devananda there, citing the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya”; but in the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” (act 9), which speaks of the seven days in Madhava Dasa's house, Devananda is not named. The version itself, however, is confirmed by the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” (Madhya 16.207–209: from Vachaspati's house to Kuliya, to the house of Madhava Dasa, for seven days) and by the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” on it, which names Devananda explicitly. Murari, it seems, speaks of the previous halt on the same journey — at Vachaspati's house.
